chapters.title: Your first programs
chapters.subtitle: From a blank page to your first output.
lesson: One small program
A C program starts in main. Instructions inside its braces run in order. A semicolon finishes most statements. return 0 tells the environment that the program finished successfully.
Give the computer a voice
Include stdio.h to use printf. Text goes between double quotes. The escape sequence \n starts a new line; it is part of the string. Output is case-sensitive.
Give it some input

scanf("%d", &value) reads an integer into an existing variable. The & means its address; we explore that later. Check scanf's return value before using the input. In this workspace, enter the complete input before pressing Run.

chapters.title: Variables & calculations
chapters.subtitle: Turn everyday information into useful results.
lesson: A name for a value
Declare an int for whole numbers or a double for fractional values. Initialise variables before reading them. Assignment (=) replaces the stored value. It is not a mathematical equation.
Choose your arithmetic
For nonnegative integers, / gives a whole-number quotient and % gives a remainder. 125 / 60 is 2; 125 % 60 is 5. Use a floating operand, such as 3.0, when you want a fractional result.
Make the output useful
printf("%d", count) prints an int. printf("%.2f", value) prints a double with two digits after the decimal point. scanf uses %lf when reading a double.

chapters.title: Making decisions
chapters.subtitle: Teach a program to choose what happens next.
lesson: Ask a yes-or-no question
A comparison such as score >= 10 produces 0 (false) or 1 (true). if runs a block when its condition is nonzero; else handles the other path. Use == to compare, not =.
Boundary values matter
When checking a threshold, try a value below it, equal to it, and above it. Order an else-if chain so each range has a single clear destination.
Combine conditions
&& means both conditions must hold; || means at least one holds. ! negates a condition. Short-circuit evaluation skips the right side when the result is already known.

chapters.title: Loops & repetition
chapters.subtitle: Let a small instruction do a lot of work.
lesson: Repeat with a plan
A for loop has initialisation, a condition checked before each iteration, and an update after each iteration. for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) visits n positions: 0 through n-1.
Carry a result forward
An accumulator remembers work across iterations. Initialise a sum to 0, or a product to 1. Then update it once for each value you process.
Know when to stop
A while loop repeats while its condition stays nonzero. Make sure something changes toward stopping. Use Stop if your experiment runs forever; your editor stays responsive.

chapters.title: Arrays & collections
chapters.subtitle: Work with a whole collection of values.
lesson: Give each value an index
int values[5] reserves five integers. The valid indexes are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. C does not automatically check bounds; going outside them is undefined behaviour.
Traverse a collection
Keep the element count separate from the capacity. Read or process elements with a loop from 0 up to, but not including, the count.
Search deliberately
A linear search visits items until it finds the target. Return its first zero-based index, or -1 if absent. Finding the largest item starts with an actual element, not an arbitrary zero.

chapters.title: Functions & decomposition
chapters.subtitle: Name a small job. Reuse it with confidence.
lesson: A named operation
A function packages an operation with a name, parameters, and return type. int twice(int x) receives a copy of x and returns an integer. Each call has its own local variables.
Keep responsibilities small
Let main handle input and output. Let a helper function calculate a result. This makes it easier to test and reason about one responsibility at a time.
Declare before calling
Place a function definition above its first use, or declare a prototype before main. A void parameter list means no parameters. An ordinary argument is passed by value.

chapters.title: Pointers & memory
chapters.subtitle: Follow an address. Change the right value.
lesson: An address, not a mystery
A pointer stores an address. int *p = &score points p at score. & obtains an address; *p accesses the value at that address. A pointer must refer to a valid live object before you dereference it.
Change a caller’s value
Passing a pointer copies the address. A function can use that copied address to modify the original object. This is why scanf needs &value.
Respect lifetime and bounds

Never dereference an uninitialised or null pointer. Never return the address of a local variable. Pointer arithmetic is valid within an array (and one past it), but you cannot dereference the one-past position.

chapters.title: Strings & text
chapters.subtitle: Read, inspect, and transform characters.
lesson: A string ends with zero
A C string is an array of char ending with a null character, \0. That terminator occupies a position, so a buffer for 40 text characters needs capacity 41.
Read within the buffer
Use fgets for whole lines. For a whitespace-free word in char word[101], scanf("%100s", word) leaves room for the terminator. An array name already gives the first element’s address here.
Walk to the terminator
Loop while text[i] != '\0'. Do not compare strings with ==; compare characters, or use strcmp once you understand how strings work. The challenges here use ASCII text.

chapters.title: Structures & records
chapters.subtitle: Keep related values together.
lesson: Describe a meaningful thing
A structure groups related members, possibly with different types. typedef struct { int x; int y; } Point creates a convenient name for a point type.
Use the member you need
For a structure value p, write p.x. For a pointer ptr to a structure, write ptr->x. Structure assignment copies its members; arrays embedded in the structure are copied too.
Separate data from behaviour
Functions can accept or return structures. Pass a pointer when you need to modify the caller’s record. Keep input validation and formatting at the boundary.

chapters.title: Dynamic memory
chapters.subtitle: Make space when you know how much you need.
lesson: Allocate at runtime
malloc(n * sizeof *items) requests room for n elements and returns a pointer or NULL. Include stdlib.h. Check the result before using it; malloc does not initialise the elements.
Give each allocation an owner
Decide which part of the program is responsible for calling free. Release memory once, after the last use. Reading after free, freeing twice, or losing the last pointer to an allocation is a bug.
Grow safely
Store realloc's result in a temporary pointer. If growth fails, the original allocation is still valid. If it succeeds, use the new pointer; the old address may no longer be valid.

chapters.title: Headers & multiple files
chapters.subtitle: Give each part of a program a clear home.
lesson: A declaration is a promise
A header describes the interface: prototypes, shared types, and constants. A .c file provides the definitions. Include your own header with double quotes.
Compile, then link
Each .c file becomes a separate object file. The linker joins them and resolves references. A function can be declared many times consistently, but normally has exactly one definition.
Protect the interface
Use an include guard: #ifndef NAME_H, #define NAME_H, the declarations, then #endif. Keep implementation details out of headers. All .c tabs in this workspace are compiled together.

chapters.title: Randomness & simulation
chapters.subtitle: Explore repeatable experiments.
lesson: Pseudorandom is reproducible
rand() produces a pseudorandom integer between 0 and RAND_MAX. srand(seed) selects a repeatable sequence for that implementation. Seed once before a simulation, not on every draw.
Map a range carefully

For a simple classroom die, 1 + rand() % 6 maps to 1–6. This has a small modulo bias; it is not a statistically perfect method or suitable for security. Exact sequences can differ between C libraries.
Test properties, not magic numbers

To test rand portably, check bounds or repeatability after reseeding. For exercises needing exact numeric outputs across compilers, use an explicitly defined generator. Our small teaching generator is (17*state + 43) % 100, not a secure or high-quality RNG.

chapters.title: Files & persistence
chapters.subtitle: Save a result. Read it back.
lesson: Open, check, use, close
fopen returns a FILE pointer, or NULL on failure. Mode "w" creates or truncates a file; "a" appends; "r" reads. Always check the pointer and close the stream after use.
Use familiar formatted operations
fprintf and fscanf are like printf and scanf, with a FILE pointer as their first argument. Check read results. fgetc returns int so it can represent every byte and EOF.
Files here are virtual

Your C program sees an in-memory filesystem. It cannot access your real disk. Each run starts fresh from the editor files; generated text files appear in the Files panel and can be downloaded. They are not automatically added to your next run.

chapters.title: Recursion & algorithms
chapters.subtitle: Solve a smaller version of the same problem.
lesson: Stop at a base case
A recursive function calls itself with a smaller problem. It must reach a base case that returns directly. Each unfinished call occupies space on the call stack.
Follow one call at a time
For factorial, fact(0) is 1 and fact(n) is n*fact(n-1). Trace the calls down to zero, then the returned results back up. Use bounded inputs to avoid integer overflow and stack exhaustion.
Choose recursion for a reason
Recursion often fits trees and divide-and-conquer algorithms. A loop may be simpler for linear repetition. Naive recursive Fibonacci repeats work exponentially; do not use it for large inputs.

chapters.title: Stacks, queues & lists
chapters.subtitle: Choose the structure that fits the job.
lesson: Last in, first out
A stack returns the most recently pushed value first. An array and a count are enough for a bounded stack. Check capacity before push and check nonempty before pop.
First in, first out
A queue returns the earliest enqueued value first. A head index and element count can describe a circular buffer; modulo arithmetic wraps an index.
Link separately allocated nodes

A linked list node stores a value and a pointer to the next node. Preserve the next pointer before freeing the current node. Know which pointer owns the chain and update it carefully when inserting or removing.

exercises.output: The sum recovered from the file.
hints: Write the steps in plain words before writing C.
Trace your variables with the example input, one statement at a time.
Check the boundary cases shown in the examples. Match the requested output exactly.
